source.title: Open-set Label Noise Can Improve Robustness Against Inherent Label Noise
source.authors: Hong-Xin Wei; Lue Tao; Renchunzi Xie; Bo An

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results on noisy-label robustness and OOD detection, but does not test the claim versions’ specified phenomena or measures.
record.gate_note: The experiments evaluate adding dynamic random labels to open-set auxiliary data during noisy-label training. Their test-accuracy results are recorded as findings about generalization under noisy labels, but they do not measure the training–test gap or the specific behaviors named in V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study uses networks' ability to memorize random labels to motivate an auxiliary regularizer, then evaluates its noisy-label robustness and OOD detection performance. It does not test any specified version. Fixed random labels are applied to auxiliary data without measuring near-perfect memorization and chance-level held-out performance; the loss-landscape plots do not test magnitude-aware sharpness against generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that ODNL improves robustness to several kinds of inherent label noise, complements existing robust-training methods, and improves OOD detection in their experiments. They also interpret ODNL as SGD noise that can lead to flatter minima.
record.recipe_differences: Adds open-set auxiliary examples with dynamic random labels to training on inherently noisy labels; evaluates test accuracy rather than the training–test gap in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect varies with auxiliary dataset size for fixed open-set random labels (Figure 1); the authors also report sensitivity to the ODNL weight η (Figure 4).

fits_no_version.finding: Adding ODNL raises test accuracy under every retained noisy-label condition on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Open-set auxiliary examples with dynamic random labels can improve classification accuracy when training labels are noisy.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 reports that sufficiently large fixed-random-label open-set auxiliary datasets become harmless with clean training labels and beneficial with inherent label noise; closed-set auxiliary noise remains harmful.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of randomly labeled auxiliary data depends on its distribution and sample size.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 depicts flatter local loss landscapes for ODNL and SLN than for Standard training and OE under symmetric-40% label noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dynamic-label regularizers can produce flatter visualized loss landscapes during noisy-label training.

record.problems: The reported table results use five trials and provide standard deviations. The study does not report the training–test gap, so its test-accuracy improvements do not establish the claim versions’ specified effects.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Table 2 results for Decoupling, F-correction, PHuber-CE, Co-teaching and JoCoR are omitted; the nine retained rows cover Standard training across the listed dataset and noise conditions. Other results, including Clothing1M, architecture comparisons, OOD metrics and figure-only plots, were not extracted because they do not directly measure a version in the claim.

untested.parts: Coexistence of near-perfect fixed-random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same recipe, including chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets and recovery strategies.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Effects of adding or removing dropout; dropout is a fixed recipe component in some experiments.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test error gaps among similarly fitted networks, including comparisons with other generalization measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The retained numerical comparisons match Tables 1–2. Their observed accuracy improvements do not establish any listed version. Lack of a training–test gap alone would not exclude all versions; the decisive issue is that the interventions and measurements do not match them. Figure 2 does not establish V7's specified correlation. E2 concerns Figure 1's fixed-label auxiliary-size experiment, not the dynamic-label comparisons in R1–R5.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization under the specified recipes.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning choices.
Batch-size comparisons and fixed-epoch generalization gaps.
Dropout intervention and its effects across training-set sizes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training–test gap.
Removal of memorized training examples and its effect on test accuracy.
